transcript.content: Hi, welcome in. I'm Dr. [Name]. To start off, can you tell me what brings you in today?

Hello, Doctor. Thank you for fitting me in. Well, it’s a little hard to explain where it all started, but I suppose what really made me come in today is that my eating has gotten all turned around. It’s just completely upside down lately. 

You know, I’ve always been someone who keeps a very regular schedule, especially since I haven't been working for years now—breakfast early, a nice sensible lunch right at noon—but lately... well, some days I just forget lunch completely. I’ll look up at the stove clock and it’s already four in the afternoon, and I haven’t even thought about making a sandwich or heating up some soup. It just completely slips my mind. 

But then, on the other hand, there are these other days where I just stand right there at the kitchen counter—not even bothering to sit down at the dining table like a normal person, just standing there—eating handfuls of crackers and whatever sweets I can find tucked away in the cupboards. And the strangest part of it all is that nothing even tastes right. I’ll be chewing on a cookie or a saltine, and it’s like dust or cardboard, just no flavor or joy in it at all, but I keep standing there eating it anyway. It’s just so out of character for me, and it’s been throwing my whole routine off, because usually I’m very particular about my meals, and I just don't understand why I'm doing it...
Besides forgetting meals, have you noticed yourself forgetting other everyday things—like appointments, names, or where you put common items—more than before?

Well, now that you mention it... no, I wouldn't say my memory is failing me in that way. It's not like I'm losing my keys or forgetting my neighbor's name or anything like that. I mean, I still have my wits about me, thank goodness. Just the other day, Mrs. Higgins from down the hall—she's been in 4B since 1998, lovely woman but she talks your ear off if you let her—she asked me if I remembered when the plumber was coming, and I knew right away it was Tuesday at 10 AM. I even remembered to remind her to move her potted ferns away from the sink. 

And my appointments, well, I have a little calendar on the refrigerator, the one with the Thomas Kinkade paintings, and I write everything down in my blue pen. I never miss a thing. I know exactly where my glasses are, I know where I left my knitting... it's just the food. It's just the eating that's so strange. I can remember to water my African violets every single Sunday morning, right after I listen to the radio program, but I just can't seem to remember to feed myself a proper lunch. It's like my brain just skips right over the idea of a meal, but everything else is right where it should be. So, no, I wouldn't say I'm getting forgetful in general, just... just this one peculiar thing with the kitchen.
Over the past couple of weeks, have you noticed feeling down, sad, or losing interest and pleasure in things you used to enjoy?

Well... yes, I suppose I have. It’s hard to put into words exactly, but most mornings lately, I wake up and there’s just this... this heavy, low feeling sitting right on my chest. It’s like the color has completely gone out of the day before I even get dressed or put my slippers on. 

I used to love mornings, you know. I’d open the curtains in the living room right away to let the sun in, maybe watch the birds at the feeder out on the balcony—I get cardinals sometimes, beautiful bright red ones, and those little chickadees that are just so busy all the time. But lately, I just sit on the edge of the bed and look at the wall, and I don't even care if the curtains stay closed all day. The thought of getting up and doing my usual things... it just feels like wading through molasses. 

Even my knitting, which I’ve done since I was a girl—my grandmother taught me, she was a wonderful knitter, made the most beautiful cable-knit sweaters for everyone in the family—I haven’t touched my needles in weeks. I have a lovely baby blanket I started for my grand-niece, just a soft pastel yellow, halfway done, sitting right there in the basket next to my armchair. But I look at it, and I just feel... nothing. No joy in it at all. It’s just this constant, dull sadness that follows me from room to room, and it’s just so exhausting to feel this way all the time. I just don't feel like myself, Doctor.
Have you been diagnosed with any medical illnesses recently, or started any new medications, before these feelings of sadness and appetite changes began?

Well, let me think... no, no new medical problems, thank goodness. Dr. Evans—he's my primary care doctor, such a nice young man, always takes the time to ask about my African violets—he hasn't found anything new. I go see him every six months like clockwork, usually in April and October. My blood pressure has always been a little on the high side, but I've been taking the same little white pill for that for, oh, it must be fifteen years now. 

And as for new medications... no, nothing like that either. I take my blood pressure pill, and my daily vitamin—the one for women over fifty, though I suppose I'm well past fifty now!—and sometimes a little calcium supplement because Dr. Evans said it's good for my bones, but I've been taking all of those for years and years. I keep them right in my little pill organizer, the one with the days of the week printed on it, right next to the toaster so I don't forget them with my breakfast. Well, when I was eating breakfast properly, anyway. But no, no new prescriptions, no new over-the-counter things, not even a new brand of herbal tea. Everything physically has been just the same as it always is, which makes this whole heavy, sad feeling and the not eating just so much more confusing to me. It just seemed to come on out of nowhere, without anything else changing at all.
How many weeks or days have you been feeling this low mood and having these changes in your eating?

Well, you know, it's funny you ask how many weeks or days, because it feels like it's been so much longer than just a few weeks. I was trying to figure this out just the other day while I was sitting in my armchair—the one by the window where I usually knit, though as I said, I haven't touched my needles in ages. I was looking out at the street, and I remembered it started right around the time Mrs. Higgins's grandson graduated from college. That was last spring, not this past spring, but the one before. Yes, it was May, because she brought over a piece of graduation cake—lemon, with that thick buttercream frosting she knows I usually love—and I remember looking at it and just feeling that heavy, gray feeling starting to settle in. 

So, if I really sit down and count it out... let's see, all of last summer, through the winter, and now here we are... it’s been about a year and two months. A year and two months of this low, colorless stretch. It’s hard to believe it’s been that long, but when I think about all the holidays that passed—Thanksgiving, Christmas, Easter—and how I just couldn't muster up the energy to care about any of them, it really has been that long. I used to make my special sweet potato casserole for Thanksgiving, the one with the pecans and brown sugar crust, but last year I just couldn't even bear the thought of turning the oven on. So yes, a year and two months, give or take a week, of just feeling like the joy has been completely drained out of everything.

During this past year or so, has there been any stretch of two months or more when your mood lifted back to normal and you felt like yourself again, or has this low, heavy feeling been continuous the entire time without any real break?

Well... let me think about that. A break... a time when I felt like myself. You know, it hasn't been just one solid, unbroken block of gray, not exactly. There was a time, maybe... oh, I think it was right after the New Year, yes, because I remember taking down the few decorations I had managed to put up, just that little tabletop tree with the silver ornaments. Anyway, there was a stretch, maybe for a few weeks, where that terrible heaviness did lift just a little bit. 

It was quite strange, really. I found myself actually getting out of my pajamas before noon, which I hadn't done in months, and I was even making myself proper lunches again—soup and a half sandwich, usually turkey on rye, instead of just nibbling on dry toast. The sadness wasn't pressing down on me quite so hard, and I remember thinking, "Oh, maybe this is it, maybe it's finally passing." 

But... and this is the part that is so hard to explain, Doctor... even though the sadness was better, and I was eating and dressing, I still didn't feel right. I still felt... well, I was still so certain about the records. You see, even when my mood was a bit lighter, I couldn't shake the knowledge that the dates and the names in the public records—the ones I look at down at the county clerk's office, or even just the ones printed in the back of the local paper—were being altered. I just knew they were being changed on purpose to send me a signal. It's like a code, you know? They shift a date here, misspell a name there, and it means something. So, even when I wasn't feeling so utterly depressed and exhausted, I was still dealing with that. The sadness took a little vacation, I suppose you could say, for those few weeks, but that feeling of being signaled through the records... that never went away at all.

Aside from that brief period after New Year's when your mood improved, has this belief that the records and dates are being deliberately changed to send you a signal been present continuously the whole time, even during weeks when you weren't feeling depressed at all?

Well, let me think about that... continuously the whole time... yes, yes, I suppose it has been. You see, the thing about the records, Doctor, is that they don't take a holiday. Even when I was feeling a bit more spry, like I mentioned, when I was making my little turkey on rye sandwiches and actually putting on my good blue cardigan instead of my bathrobe—even then, I would open the Tuesday edition of the local paper, the one that lists the property transfers and the minor court dockets, and there it would be. 

I remember one morning specifically, it must have been mid-January, because it was terribly cold and the frost was just thick on my front window. I was sitting at the kitchen table, having a cup of Earl Grey—I had actually bothered to steep it properly in the pot, not just a bag in a mug—and I was looking at the public notices section. And right there, they had listed a property transfer for a house on Elm Street, but they put the date as the 14th instead of the 12th. And the buyer's last name had an extra 'e' on the end. Now, to anyone else, to Mrs. Higgins next door or to my nephew if he ever bothered to visit, they would just think it was a typo. A careless typesetter down at the paper. 

But I know better. I could feel it, right in the pit of my stomach, even though I wasn't feeling that heavy, awful sadness that day. I knew it was a signal. It’s like a thread that runs through everything, you know? The sadness comes and goes—well, mostly it stays, but it did go that one time—but the thread, the signals... they never stop. I check the county clerk's website on my tablet, too. My nephew bought me that tablet for my seventieth birthday, said it would keep my mind sharp. Well, it certainly does that! I check the deed recordings, and the marriage licenses, and it's always there. A number shifted, a name altered. It’s a constant stream of messages, just beneath the surface of things. So, yes, to answer your question, even during those few weeks when the dark cloud lifted and I thought maybe I was getting my life back, the signals in the records were still there, clear as day to me, never stopping for a moment.

You see, even when my mood was a bit lighter, I couldn't shake the knowledge that the dates and the names in the public records—the ones I look at down at the county clerk's office, or even just the ones printed in the back of the local paper—were being altered. I just knew they were being changed on purpose to send me a signal. It's like a code, you know? They shift a date here, misspell a name there, and it means something. So, even when I wasn't feeling so utterly depressed and exhausted, I was still dealing with that. The sadness took a little vacation, I suppose you could say, for those few weeks, but that feeling of being signaled through the records... that never went away at all.

inference.note: The patient reports a persecutory/referential delusion (belief that public records are being altered as coded signals) that persisted even during a period when her depressive mood clearly lifted for several weeks. This indicates psychotic symptoms occurring independently of the mood episode, which is inconsistent with simple MDD (F32.9/F33.9) or persistent depressive disorder (F34.1) and instead points toward a schizoaffective process or a depressive disorder with psychotic features.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the delusional belief about records being altered has persisted continuously and independently of mood episodes, including periods of normal mood, to distinguish psychotic depression from a schizoaffective process
doctor.question: Aside from that brief period after New Year's when your mood improved, has this belief that the records and dates are being deliberately changed to send you a signal been present continuously the whole time, even during weeks when you weren't feeling depressed at all?

patient.answer:
Well, let me think about that... continuously the whole time... yes, yes, I suppose it has been. You see, the thing about the records, Doctor, is that they don't take a holiday. Even when I was feeling a bit more spry, like I mentioned, when I was making my little turkey on rye sandwiches and actually putting on my good blue cardigan instead of my bathrobe—even then, I would open the Tuesday edition of the local paper, the one that lists the property transfers and the minor court dockets, and there it would be. 

I remember one morning specifically, it must have been mid-January, because it was terribly cold and the frost was just thick on my front window. I was sitting at the kitchen table, having a cup of Earl Grey—I had actually bothered to steep it properly in the pot, not just a bag in a mug—and I was looking at the public notices section. And right there, they had listed a property transfer for a house on Elm Street, but they put the date as the 14th instead of the 12th. And the buyer's last name had an extra 'e' on the end. Now, to anyone else, to Mrs. Higgins next door or to my nephew if he ever bothered to visit, they would just think it was a typo. A careless typesetter down at the paper. 

But I know better. I could feel it, right in the pit of my stomach, even though I wasn't feeling that heavy, awful sadness that day. I knew it was a signal. It’s like a thread that runs through everything, you know? The sadness comes and goes—well, mostly it stays, but it did go that one time—but the thread, the signals... they never stop. I check the county clerk's website on my tablet, too. My nephew bought me that tablet for my seventieth birthday, said it would keep my mind sharp. Well, it certainly does that! I check the deed recordings, and the marriage licenses, and it's always there. A number shifted, a name altered. It’s a constant stream of messages, just beneath the surface of things. So, yes, to answer your question, even during those few weeks when the dark cloud lifted and I thought maybe I was getting my life back, the signals in the records were still there, clear as day to me, never stopping for a moment.

inference.note: Patient reports the paranoid delusion about altered records persisted even during a several-week period when her depressive mood fully remitted, confirming psychotic symptoms occur independent of the mood episode. This rules out F32.3 and F33.3 (major depressive disorder with psychotic features, where psychosis should only occur during mood episodes) and supports schizoaffective disorder, depressive type (F25.1).

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient reports a prolonged (~14 month) major depressive episode with pervasive anhedonia, low mood, psychomotor slowing, and disturbed eating pattern (skipping meals, anhedonic snacking with loss of taste pleasure), meeting criteria for a major depressive episode. Throughout this period, and critically during a distinct several-week interval when mood fully normalized (improved energy, appetite, dressing, activity), the patient continued to hold a fixed, non-bizarre-but-clearly-delusional belief that public records/dates were being deliberately altered to send her personal coded signals (ideas of reference/persecutory delusion). Because the psychotic symptom persisted for at least 2 weeks in the clear absence of a mood episode, this satisfies Criterion B for schizoaffective disorder rather than MDD with psychotic features (which requires psychosis only during mood episodes). Because mood symptoms were present for the great majority of the total illness duration (roughly 12 of ~14 months), depressive type schizoaffective disorder (F25.1) is the best fit over schizophrenia (F20.9), which would require mood episodes to be brief relative to psychotic duration.
